news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire to bring in new special school funding bands from the autumn 2026 term
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire's special schools will be funded under a new banding model from the autumn 2026 term, according to papers for the county's Schools' Forum meeting on 8 October. Banding sets the funding a school receives according to the level of need among its pupils.

The papers, an update on reforms to support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), say the review of the framework has been "progressed and concluded". The new model was developed with special school leaders and finance colleagues. It is meant to line funding up more closely with need, so that banding and funding "more accurately reflect need from the outset".

A key aim, the paper says, is to reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements, those that sit outside the standard bands. It also links the change to the long-term financial sustainability of the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The papers give no figures for what the new model will cost or save.

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire schools grant overspent by £23.0m in 2025/26, pushing its reserve negative for first time
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council overspent its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £23.0 million in 2025/26, according to a value for money risk assessment before its Audit Committee on 21 September. The year was the first in which the grant's reserve moved into a negative position.

The paper attributes the overspend principally to the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. It says this reflects "a continued increase in the number of children and young people requiring specialist educational support and services." The paper describes the deficit as a structural demand pressure that persists, rather than a one-year variation.

The council has set up arrangements to review how effective its high needs spending is. The paper does not give a figure for the total deficit now carried on the grant, a date by which the overspend is expected to stop, or the amount the review is expected to save.
news_drafts.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire County Council's schools grant overspent by £13.406m in 2025-26, leaving a £25.005m deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council overspent its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £13.406m in 2025-26, according to its review of financial performance for the year. Excluding school balances, the paper puts the deficit carried forward at £25.005m, which it describes as structural.

The paper attributes the overspend to "continued pressure within the High Needs block". High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The paper says government will support approximately 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026, but only if the council submits an approved plan for reforming support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). Any amount the government does not cover must be managed through the council's future financial planning, the paper says.

The papers given to the desk do not say how much of the £25.005m the 90% would cover, or when the council expects to submit its SEND reform plan.

findings.headline: Head of Governance and Business Development at WYPF departing at end of October 2026
findings.detail: Matt Mott, Head of Governance and Business Development, is leaving WYPF at the end of October 2026. This senior role is responsible for governance updates to pension board meetings and oversight of major regulatory initiatives including McCloud, Pensions Dashboard and Pensions Regulator liaison. Recruitment for a replacement is open with a closing date of 11 October 2026.
findings.matters: Departure of senior governance leadership affects continuity of oversight during major regulatory programmes; a finance director or peer council monitors leadership changes at shared service providers as an indicator of organizational stability.
findings.figures: Departure end of October 2026, recruitment closing date 11 October 2026
findings.quote: Matthew Mott will be leaving West Yorkshire Pension Fund at the end of October.

findings.headline: Life Certificates internal audit rated control environment as partially effective with three improvement recommendations
findings.detail: Bradford Councils Internal Audit review of WYPF Life Certificates determined that control of identified risks is only partially effective. The audit found that 'a number of the risks examined are not effectively managed' and that 'the control environment would benefit from significant improvement to support the achievement of key business objectives'. Three recommendations were made for improvement and have been or will be implemented by management. Life Certificates are an anti-fraud control ensuring payments to deceased pensioners are identified and stopped.
findings.matters: An audit rating below effective indicates control gaps in a critical process; a finance director would want to track implementation of recommendations and monitor whether the next audit cycle shows improvement.
findings.quote: It is audit's opinion that the standard of control of identified risks in the system is partially effective.

findings.headline: Pension administration management expenses forecast to underspend by £0.66m in 2026/27 with cost per member £1.70 below budget
findings.detail: Management expense forecast for 2026/27 is £12.00m against budget of £12.66m, delivering an underspend of £0.66m. Cost per member forecast at £22.53 versus budgeted £24.23, a saving of £1.70 per member. The favourable variance is driven by membership standing at 532,776 against a budget assumption of 522,610—approximately 10,000 members higher than forecast, spreading fixed costs more efficiently. Over five years to 2031/32, costs are forecast to rise from £12.66m to £13.98m, an average annual increase of approximately 2%.
findings.matters: A material budget variance driven by demand growth is relevant to how a finance director assesses shared service value for money and long-term cost sustainability; the cost-per-member efficiency gain demonstrates the benefit of demand growth.
findings.figures: Forecast £12.00m vs budget £12.66m = underspend £0.66m; cost per member £22.53 vs £24.23 = £1.70 saving; membership 532,776 vs budget 522,610; five-year forecast £12.66m (2026/27) to £13.98m (2031/32)
findings.quote: The management expense forecast for 2026/27 is £12.00m, compared with a budget of £12.66m, resulting in an underspend of £0.66m.

findings.headline: McCloud retrospective pension recalculations not completed by 31 August 2026 regulatory deadline due to late software release from Civica
findings.detail: Software for retrospective pension recalculations required under McCloud remedy was not delivered until 7 August, making testing impossible before the statutory 31 August deadline. WYPF identified approximately 6,331 Lincolnshire pensioners with McCloud protection; based on experience processing new retirements, estimates approximately 405 (6.4%) will require underpin adjustment. WYPF acknowledged it should have informed Shared Service partners earlier of the risk when June delivery dates were missed. Further releases expected late 2026 and early 2027 for complex cases including deaths, transfers and divorces.
findings.matters: Missing a statutory deadline for pension benefit calculations is material; the failure to communicate the risk to partners earlier reflects governance control issues relevant to a lender's assessment of management quality.
findings.figures: Deadline 31 August 2026, software delivered 7 August, 6,331 pensioners with protection identified, approximately 405 estimated to require adjustment, 6.4% observed adjustment rate
findings.quote: The release was eventually issued by Civica on 7 August but required testing before being deployed to the live environment. This was not possible to complete before the 31 August deadline.

findings.headline: Five pension administration KPI targets missed in quarter ending 30 June 2026, with Interfund Out Actual at 66.67%
findings.detail: Five work types failed to meet performance targets in Q1 2026/27: Deferred Benefits Into Payment Quote 78.95%, Interfund Linking In Actual 79.17%, Interfund Out Actual 66.67%, Interfund Out Quote 82.02%, and Monthly Posting 78.13%. Root causes include two experienced staff promoted from Team Linkings creating training backlog for new role holders, staffing vacancies being filled, suspension of transfer factors due to SCAPE, and MP3 system processing delays. All are Priority 2 (medium importance).
findings.matters: A finance director monitors whether pension administration shared services meet service commitments and whether staffing or system issues present risks to compliance or service quality.
findings.figures: Interfund Out Actual 66.67%, Interfund Linking In 79.17%, Deferred Benefits 78.95%, Monthly Posting 78.13%, Interfund Out Quote 82.02%
findings.quote: Was not met as Team Linkings have just taken over this area of work and we are in the process of training staff to be able to do and check all process types. We have lost two experienced staff to promotion.
